headline: Democrats win both chambers, the Senate by the narrowest margin: 51–49, decided in Ohio
scenario: The polls get the national mood right: Democrats win the House vote by about 9 points. But the races revert toward their states' partisanship, as they did in 2018, 2022 and 2024. Democrats and independents run behind their polls in deep-red Kansas, Iowa, Alaska, Nebraska and South Carolina, and a little ahead of them in swing and blue states. That leaves the Senate on a knife-edge and gives Democrats a good night for governors.

races.label: Alaska
races.why: Sullivan wins after ranked-choice transfers from the two other Republicans. Alaska polls overstated Democrats in 2020 and 2024.

races.label: Florida
races.why: Florida's polls overstated Democrats by 6 to 8 points in 2022 and 2024.

races.label: Iowa
races.why: Hinson holds. Iowa's final polls overstated the Democrat in 2018, 2020 and 2024, and Turek's lead is under 2 points.

races.label: Kansas
races.why: Marshall holds despite trailing in all six polls of the final week. In federal races, Kansas polls overstated the Democrat by 6 or 7 points in 2020 and 2024.

races.label: Maine
races.why: Jackson by 2, half his polling lead. Collins beat her final polls by more than 10 points in 2020.

races.label: Nebraska
races.why: Osborn falls short again: his 2024 polls ran about 5 points ahead of his result.

races.label: Ohio
races.why: Brown by under a point, the seat that decides the Senate. He leads almost every final poll, including Trafalgar's, but Ohio's final polls have overstated the Democrat in every statewide race since 2018.

races.label: South Carolina
races.why: South Carolina's Senate polls showed a close race in 2020 too, and the Republican won by 10.

races.label: Texas
races.why: Talarico narrowly. Texas polls overstated Democrats by 3 to 5 points in 2020-24, but Paxton runs well behind the rest of his ticket.

races.label: Alaska
races.why: Kreiss-Tomkins wins the ranked-choice final round, with a smaller lead than in the Times/Siena poll.

races.label: Georgia
races.why: Bottoms narrowly, possibly only in a December 1 runoff (Georgia needs a majority).

races.label: Kansas
races.why: Masterson holds the open seat, though Kansas Democrats beat their governor polls in 2018 and 2022.

races.label: Nevada
races.why: Ford beats Lombardo. Democrats banked a 5.9-point lead in ballots, with 50% Democratic turnout against 43% Republican, and Nevada Democrats beat their final polls in the last Trump midterm. The forecast finds no skill in early-vote composition; this race tests that.

races.label: Oregon
races.why: Kotek beat her final polls by about 3 points in 2022 and does again.

races.label: Vermont
races.why: The forecast's coin flip goes to Janoo, who leads the polls. In a wave against the president's party, Vermont's 33-point Democratic lean finally catches up with its popular Republican governor.

bold.title: Kansas, Iowa and Alaska stay Republican
bold.why: The forecast leans Democratic in all three (55 to 61%). Federal races in deep-red states have broken late for the home team: Indiana, Missouri and Tennessee in 2018, Iowa, Kansas and Alaska in 2020, and everywhere in 2024.

bold.title: Ohio decides the Senate
bold.why: Democrats need 51 seats. Brown's win by under a point is the 51st, so the majority is the smallest possible.

bold.title: Ford ousts Lombardo in Nevada
bold.why: Called against the forecast (29%), on the early vote's Democratic lean. The forecast finds early-vote composition adds nothing to the polls; Nevada tests it.

bold.title: Phil Scott's run ends in Vermont
bold.why: Five-term Republican governor of a state 33 points more Democratic than the nation, beaten in a wave against his party's president.

bold.title: Collins beats her polls, but not by enough
bold.why: Jackson wins by 2, half his polling lead, and the Democrats' majority rests on Maine as well as Ohio.

rcv.note: Most of the two other Republicans' ballots transfer to Sullivan. Alaska counts until about November 18.
Kreiss-Tomkins leads the first round by 15 points and holds on as the Republicans' transfers close the gap.
